content: Research is essential to identify interventions that improve outcomes for various groups of adolescents and young adults living with HIV. These groups include individuals with disabilities, those with mental health conditions, those who acquired HIV perinatally versus horizontally, younger adolescents, those out of school, orphans, ethnic minority groups, key populations, pregnant individuals, and those living in adverse conditions such as extreme poverty or humanitarian emergencies. Additionally, research is needed to explore the content and delivery strategies of interventions that involve parents and caregivers for both younger and older adolescents, as well as to evaluate the effectiveness of these programs. Further research is required to develop feasible and effective training, supervision, and implementation models for scaling up psychosocial interventions, including those delivered by peer providers. There is also a pressing need for research and program evaluation in resource-limited settings to assess psychosocial interventions for these populations. This would be enhanced by collecting more data on the costs and cost-effectiveness of such interventions. To improve implementation, intervention studies should include methods to capture and report costs. Long-term follow-up beyond the immediate post-intervention period is also necessary to fully understand the sustained impact of psychosocial interventions. Task-sharing of specimen collection and point-of-care testing with non-laboratory personnel should be implemented in settings with limited professional staffing capacity. This recommendation is strongly supported by moderate-certainty evidence. In 2016, the WHO guidelines stated that trained and supervised non-laboratory personnel, including laypeople, could safely perform blood finger-prick sampling. Since then, additional studies have demonstrated the diagnostic accuracy and clinical impact of decentralized and task-shared specimen collection and testing by non-laboratory personnel. These findings support the use of point-of-care infant diagnosis and viral load testing to improve health outcomes. In many settings, trained lay health-care providers are already conducting HIV testing and sample collection using finger-prick methods. WHO strongly recommends that trained and supervised lay providers independently conduct safe and effective HIV testing using rapid diagnostic tests. Access to diagnostic testing and sample collection remains low in many resource-limited settings, particularly in rural areas, due to shortages of skilled laboratory professionals. Task-sharing of point-of-care diagnostic testing and sample collection with lower-level health-care workers may address these challenges, increase access to testing for key populations, and reduce reliance on traditional health-care services. A systematic review identified 65 studies, primarily from Africa, that evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of point-of-care testing by non-laboratory personnel. The evidence showed moderate certainty, with diagnostic accuracy exceeding 98% sensitivity and 99% specificity in many cases. Task-sharing was found to be feasible and acceptable, with non-laboratory personnel performing comparably to laboratory professionals in various diagnostic tests. Point-of-care testing significantly reduced the time to deliver results to caregivers, with same-day results achieved in 97% of cases compared to 0% for standard care. Laboratory-based testing often required a median of 35 days for caregivers to receive results. Studies also demonstrated that point-of-care testing by non-laboratory personnel was feasible, accurate, and accelerated the initiation of prophylaxis and treatment for HIV-associated infections. Task-sharing of specimen collection and testing was found to be cost-effective, with the primary costs being training, supervision, and remuneration of non-laboratory personnel, which are lower than those for laboratory professionals. Diagnostic integration across disease programs, such as HIV and tuberculosis (TB), is a promising approach to optimize resources and improve care. Integrated diagnostic networks can increase access to testing, improve patient care pathways, and reduce costs by sharing devices, operational knowledge, and resources. Several countries have successfully implemented diagnostic integration, demonstrating benefits such as faster turnaround times, increased treatment initiation rates, and improved clinical outcomes. Challenges include adjusting laboratory workflows, ensuring adequate human resources, and maintaining infrastructure and quality assurance. WHO emphasizes the importance of expanding access to high-quality diagnostic testing through integrated laboratory networks that combine laboratory-based and point-of-care technologies. Careful planning, coordination, and political will are essential for successful implementation. Further research is needed to evaluate the impact of diagnostic integration across diseases and to identify best practices for sustainable delivery of integrated diagnostic services. These updated guidelines will be made available on the WHO HIV website, with key findings and recommendations released in a policy brief. Comprehensive updates to the consolidated guidelines, including treatment and service delivery components, are planned for publication in mid-2021.
